title: The Monolith Pipeline

scenario.situation: A single nightly ETL job with 60+ sequential steps fails at step 40 on average twice a week, forcing a full rerun from step 1. Each full rerun takes 4 hours and delays downstream reports.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The engineering team is convinced the fix is adding more robust try/except error handling and retry logic inside the existing script.
scenario.question: Is more error handling really the right intervention, or is there a structural problem?

decisions.prompt: The team wants to start patching error handling immediately. How do you frame your investigation before touching any code?

options.label: Audit the existing error handling
options.detail: Review every try/except block and retry decorator in the script to find gaps.
options.consequence: You find several unhandled exceptions and add wrappers around them. Failures become quieter but the job still reruns from step 1 when anything breaks — you've treated the symptom, not the structure.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the team's hypothesis and improved optics without reducing rerun cost.

options.label: Blast-radius diagnostic
options.detail: Map each failure to which steps were already complete and quantify how much work is thrown away per failure.
options.consequence: You discover that on average 39 already-successful steps are discarded per failure. The investigation now has a structural angle the error-handling hypothesis never surfaced.

options.label: Interview the on-call engineers
options.detail: Talk to whoever pages on failures to understand what they do during incidents.
options.consequence: You learn the on-call process is painful and ad-hoc, which is useful color, but you leave without quantitative evidence of where time is actually lost or which structural change would help most.
options.divergenceCost: Chose qualitative interviews when the failure logs already contained the quantitative answer.

options.label: Benchmark against a best-practice pipeline
options.detail: Find a reference architecture online and compare the current script to it.
options.consequence: You produce a gap analysis that correctly identifies DAG patterns as best practice, but without data on Settleworks' own failure profile you can't make a compelling internal business case for the refactor.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to external benchmarking before establishing the internal cost of the status quo.

decisions.prompt: You pull two weeks of failure logs. Which metric do you use to quantify the real cost of the current architecture?

artifact.title: Failure count by step bucket — last 14 nights
artifact.caption: Raw failure counts per step range. Most failures cluster in steps 31–45 — but does knowing *where* failures happen tell you how much work they erase?

options.label: Failure count by step bucket
options.detail: Count how many failures occurred in each portion of the pipeline.
options.consequence: You see failures cluster in the middle of the job. But this metric says nothing about how many already-complete steps are wasted per failure — a late failure that discards 55 steps looks identical to an early one that discards 5.
options.divergenceCost: Counted where failures happen instead of how much completed work each failure destroys.

options.label: Wasted-step-hours per failure (normalized rerun cost)
options.detail: For each failure, multiply the steps already completed by their average runtime to get the work discarded.
options.consequence: Normalized by completed work, the picture flips: a single mid-pipeline failure wastes more engineer-equivalent compute than six early failures combined, and the all-or-nothing rerun policy is the structural multiplier driving total delay.

artifact.title: Wasted step-hours per failure event — last 14 nights
artifact.caption: Each bar = avg hours of already-completed work discarded per failure. Mid-pipeline failures erase the most work — and better error handling changes none of these numbers.

decisions.prompt: Wasted-step-hours show the monolithic rerun policy — not missing error handling — drives the delay cost. What do you tell the team?

options.label: "Error handling won't help — we need to rewrite this as a DAG immediately."
options.detail: Make the structural call and push for a full refactor.
options.consequence: You're directionally right, but you've presented a correlation as a settled cause and skipped the question of whether a DAG refactor is feasible on the current schedule. The team may push back or scope-creep into a months-long rewrite.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed certainty and skipped validating feasibility before recommending a large structural change.

options.label: "The wasted-step-hours data points to architecture, not error handling, as the cost driver — let's pilot decomposing one high-risk step range into an idempotent task before committing to a full DAG refactor."
options.detail: Present the finding, name the structural hypothesis, and propose a scoped pilot to confirm.
options.consequence: You've reframed the team's assumption with quantitative evidence, preserved their ability to validate the fix at low risk, and created a clear before/after comparison. A scoped pilot protects the team if the refactor surfaces unexpected complexity.

insight: The real problem wasn't missing error handling — it was that a monolithic all-or-nothing job turns every mid-pipeline failure into a maximum-blast-radius event, discarding hours of already-completed work. The wasted-step-hours metric makes this structural cost visible in a way raw failure counts never could. The lesson is architectural: modular, idempotent tasks let a pipeline retry only what failed, collapsing blast radius from the whole job to a single node. Sound framing meant resisting the team's hypothesis long enough to measure what the failure was actually destroying.
